items.question: "Though he ruled for barely five years, Sher Shah Suri laid the administrative foundations on which the Mughal Empire was later built." Examine.
items.modelAnswer:
The Afghan ruler **Sher Shah Suri (1540-45)**, who briefly displaced Humayun, compressed into five years a body of reforms so effective that **Akbar and even the British** later borrowed from them, justifying Humayun's tribute to him as **'Ustad-i-Badshahan' (Teacher of Kings)**.

**Revenue administration.** Sher Shah introduced a scientific system: land was **measured and classified** (good, bad, middling), the state share fixed at **one-third of produce** payable in cash or kind, and every peasant issued a **patta (title deed)** while giving a **kabuliyat (agreement)**. This direct, documented relationship between state and cultivator directly anticipated **Todar Mal's Dahsala/Zabti** under Akbar.

**Administrative structure.** The empire was divided into **sarkars** and **parganas** with clearly demarcated officers — **shiqdar** (law and order), **munsif/amin** (revenue), **fotedar** (treasurer) and **karkun** (accountant) — a template Akbar's sarkar-level faujdar and amalguzar echoed.

**Economy and communication.** He standardised the **silver rupiya and copper dam** (the rupee survived for centuries), restored the **Grand Trunk Road** from Bengal towards the north-west, and built **sarais (inns)** that doubled as post-stages, boosting trade and security. His military checks — **dagh (branding of horses)** and **chehra (descriptive rolls)**, borrowed from Alauddin Khalji — were also revived by Akbar.

**Justice and welfare.** He treated Hindus and Muslims impartially in appointments and administered justice strictly, prioritising peasant welfare.

**Conclusion.** Sher Shah's genius lay in fusing **strong central authority with humane, systematic administration**. That his currency, roads and revenue methods outlived his short dynasty confirms that the Mughal 'golden age' of governance rested substantially on Afghan foundations.
keyPoints: Ruled only 1540-45 yet reforms outlived the Sur dynasty; Humayun called him 'Teacher of Kings'.
Revenue: land measured/classified, one-third share, patta and kabuliyat — model for Todar Mal's Dahsala.
Administrative units: sarkar and pargana with shiqdar, munsif/amin, fotedar, karkun.
Economy: silver rupiya and copper dam, restored Grand Trunk Road, built sarais.
Military: revived dagh (horse branding) and chehra (descriptive rolls) from Alauddin Khalji.
Legacy: reforms adopted by Akbar and later the British revenue system.

items.question: Discuss Akbar's religious and administrative policies as instruments of consolidating a stable, inclusive empire.
items.modelAnswer:
**Akbar (1556-1605)** transformed a fragile inheritance into a durable empire by pairing **political integration** with a policy of **religious accommodation**, making the state broad enough to command the loyalty of a diverse population.

**Religious policy as statecraft.** Akbar abolished the **jizya** on non-Muslims and the pilgrimage tax, removing a fiscal and symbolic grievance. He propagated **Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace)**, held interfaith debates at the **Ibadat Khana** with Hindus, Jains, Christians and Zoroastrians, and founded the syncretic **Din-i-Ilahi (1582)**. Though the new faith won few adherents, these steps signalled that the throne stood **above any single creed** — reinforced by **matrimonial alliances with Rajput houses** and their induction as trusted generals such as **Raja Man Singh**.

**Administrative consolidation.** The **Mansabdari system** created a unified imperial service in which every officer held a numerical rank (**Zat** for status, **Sawar** for cavalry), binding nobles directly to the emperor and curbing hereditary power. The **Dahsala/Zabti** revenue system (Todar Mal's Bandobast) fixed demand on the **ten-year average of produce and prices**, giving the peasant predictability and the treasury stability, supported by **taccavi loans** for cultivation.

**Institutional memory.** Abul Fazl's **Akbarnama** and its **Ain-i-Akbari** documented this machinery, embedding it as a model for successors.

**AP/Deccan angle.** Akbar's Deccan campaigns opened the southern frontier that his successors pushed towards **Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda** — the last a Telugu-region power — showing how his consolidation set the stage for later Mughal expansion into the Andhra country.

**Conclusion.** By marrying **tolerance with tight administrative control**, Akbar built an empire whose legitimacy rested on inclusion rather than conquest alone — the very foundation whose later abandonment under Aurangzeb contributed to decline.
keyPoints: Abolished jizya and pilgrimage tax; promoted Sulh-i-Kul; founded Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
Rajput matrimonial alliances and inclusion of nobles like Man Singh broadened the base.
Mansabdari (Zat and Sawar ranks) bound nobles to the emperor and curbed hereditary power.
Dahsala/Zabti fixed revenue on ten-year averages; taccavi loans aided peasants.
Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari (Abul Fazl) recorded the administrative model.
Deccan campaigns opened the frontier later extended to Golconda (Telugu region).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Akbar

items.question: "The Mughal Empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb, yet his reign sowed the seeds of its collapse." Critically analyse the causes of Mughal decline.
items.modelAnswer:
The Mughal Empire attained its **maximum territorial extent** under **Aurangzeb (1658-1707)**, with the annexation of **Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87)**, yet within decades of his death it disintegrated — a paradox rooted partly in his own policies and partly in deeper structural strains.

**Aurangzeb's contribution to decline.** His **re-imposition of jizya (1679)**, ban on court music, and orthodox measures alienated Hindus, Rajputs and Sikhs (the execution of **Guru Tegh Bahadur, 1675**). The endless **Deccan wars against the Marathas** became a 'running ulcer' that drained the treasury and kept the emperor absent from the north for over two decades, while **guerrilla resistance** could not be crushed.

**Structural and institutional causes.** A **depleted treasury** and a **jagirdari crisis** — too many nobles chasing too few revenue assignments — bred factionalism between **Irani and Turani** groups. Weak successors became **puppets of nobles**; the **Sayyid Brothers** made and unmade emperors, and **Farrukhsiyar** became the first emperor murdered by his nobles.

**External shocks.** **Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi (1739, Battle of Karnal)** carried off the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor, and **Ahmad Shah Abdali's** repeated raids shattered prestige. Governors of **Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh** turned independent, and the **Marathas** became the paramount power until 1761.

**AP/Deccan angle.** The very Deccan conquest that marked the empire's peak — including Andhra's **Qutb Shahi Golconda** — overstretched it; the region soon slipped to the **Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad**, illustrating how imperial reach outran administrative grasp.

**Conclusion.** Mughal decline was thus **multi-causal** — Aurangzeb's religious and Deccan policies accelerated a collapse already latent in fiscal exhaustion, factional nobility and the rise of regional powers. Territorial size, unmatched by administrative and financial consolidation, proved a source of weakness rather than strength.
keyPoints: Empire peaked with Bijapur-Golconda annexation (1686-87) but collapsed after 1707.
Jizya (1679), orthodoxy and Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution alienated key communities.
Costly, unwinnable Deccan/Maratha wars drained the treasury (the 'Deccan ulcer').
Structural crises: empty treasury, jagirdari crisis, Irani-Turani noble factionalism.
Weak later Mughals were puppets; Sayyid Brothers were king-makers; Farrukhsiyar murdered by nobles.
External shocks: Nadir Shah (1739) and Abdali; Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh and Marathas broke away.
